faq.answer: No. Checklists may reflect regulated work, memory support, shared coordination, recent failure, or anxiety about consequences. Compare who created the checklist, what risk it addresses, and whether preparation persists when conditions become safer.
faq.question: Does keeping detailed checklists establish self-preservation Type One?

faq.answer: Hold the task constant. Observe whether attention first moves to resources and maintenance, shared standards and exemplary conduct, or direct reform of a particular person or bond. Repeat the comparison and retain mixed or contradictory events.
faq.question: How should the three Type One subtypes be compared?

faq.answer: Repeated ease with improvisation, neglected upkeep, flexible reserves, or stronger attention to public rules or one-to-one reform would weaken it. Material security, role demands, and learned safety routines should be tested before a subtype explanation.
faq.question: What would weaken the preparation hypothesis?

sections.body_md: The subtype hypothesis combines Type One correction concerns with a self-preservation label for attention to upkeep, sufficiency, and preventable risk. It remains descriptive and provisional; careful preparation can arise from scarcity, professional safety rules, disability access, caregiving, or recent disruption.
sections.title: Frame preparation as a traditional hypothesis

sections.body_md: A matched comparison separates preparation from social standard-setting by asking whether attention first goes to supplies and maintenance or to shared rules and exemplars. It also contrasts one-to-one reform pressure by asking whether energy first targets a particular relationship or person.
sections.title: Use the same task across three subtypes

sections.body_md: Self-preservation here is traditional vocabulary for organizing observations. It is not a measurable biological drive. It is not a neurological system. It does not assign a fixed capacity, establish survival wiring, define health status, or impose one automatic priority on every person.
sections.title: Do not reify an instinct label

sections.body_md: Subtype schools differ in descriptions and in which combinations appear countertypical. Rather than treating one presentation as canonical, record the specific preparation claim, the setting, and disconfirming events, then compare whether another school or plain environmental explanation fits better.
sections.title: Expect tradition and countertype variation

sections.body_md: Housing instability, medical routines, regulated work, caring for dependents, tight budgets, and recent equipment failure can all heighten preparation. Change the material condition or compare a safer period before attributing maintenance behavior to a subtype.
sections.title: Compare material and role conditions

sections.body_md: An environmental counterexample weakens a self-preservation One hypothesis when the person repeatedly improvises comfortably, neglects routine upkeep despite clear standards, or prioritizes public rules and intense one-person reform over resources in matched situations.
sections.title: Let improvisation challenge the subtype

sections.body_md: Evidence is instrument-specific and cannot establish a universal subtype ontology or cross-cultural equivalence. The draft offers no product-specific measurement evidence and no basis for health, personality, or outcome conclusions; every declared review and release state remains unchanged.
sections.title: Keep subtype evidence narrow

sections.body_md:
Duration: 6

Context: Choose one household maintenance task, one work contingency, and one resource decision that each have a visible standard and consequence.

Observable signal: Record the first risk named, the reserve or checklist chosen, the maintenance action completed, and what another participant observed.

Page-specific signal: Compare whether attention first targets material sufficiency, shared rules, or direct reform of one person while the practical task stays similar.

Alternative explanation: Test scarcity, regulated duties, access needs, caregiving, recent failure, budget pressure, and learned safety routines against the subtype hypothesis.

Reflection prompt: Select the event with the least preparation and explain whether improvisation, security, social standards, or one-to-one urgency fits it better.
